instrument.full_name: Treaty between the United States of America, the British Empire, France, Italy and Japan for the Limitation of Naval Armament
instrument.adopted_at: Washington, Conference on the Limitation of Armament (signed at the seventh plenary session, Memorial Continental Hall, 6 February 1922)
instrument.depositary: Government of the United States of America. Ratifications are deposited at Washington and the original, of which the French and English texts are both authentic, is kept in the archives of the United States Government, which transmits certified copies and the proces-verbal of deposit (Art. XXIV). Notices of termination are communicated in writing to the United States Government, which transmits a certified copy to the other Powers and informs them of the date of receipt (Art. XXIII).
instrument.key_non_parties: The Treaty was closed to the five Powers invited to the naval talks and has no accession clause. Belgium, China, the Netherlands and Portugal took part in the Washington Conference only for the Pacific and Far Eastern questions and did not sign it (Office of the Historian; the record of signature at the seventh plenary session lists the treaties each delegation signed, Senate Doc. 126, p. 231). Arts. XV to XVIII regulate warship construction for, and transfers to, non-Contracting Powers but give them no rights or functions.
instrument.duration_clause: Art. XXIII: "The present Treaty shall remain in force until the 31st December, 1936, and in case none of the Contracting Powers shall have given notice two years before that date of its intention to terminate the Treaty, it shall continue in force until the expiration of two years from the date on which notice of termination shall be given by one of the Contracting Powers, whereupon the Treaty shall terminate as regards all the Contracting Powers." The term is fixed by a date, not by a number of years. Japan gave notice on 29 December 1934, and the Treaty terminated on 31 December 1936 (Bevans, vol. 2, p. 351).
instrument.extension_clause: If no Contracting Power gave notice two years before 31 December 1936, the Treaty would have continued in force without further act until two years after a notice of termination by any Power (Art. XXIII). No continuation occurred, because Japan's notice of 29 December 1934 was given before that deadline (FRUS 1934, vol. I, pp. 415-416).
instrument.withdrawal_clause: There is no withdrawal of a single Power. A notice of termination by any Power, given in writing to the United States Government, ends the Treaty for all Contracting Powers: at 31 December 1936 if given at least two years before that date, otherwise two years after the notice. The notice takes effect on the date the United States Government receives it, or, for a United States notice, on its communication to the other Powers' diplomatic representatives at Washington; all Powers must meet in conference within one year of a notice taking effect (Art. XXIII). Separately, a Power at war that it considers affects its naval defence may, after notice, suspend its obligations other than those under Arts. XIII and XVII for the period of hostilities; the others then consult and, failing agreement, may also suspend (Art. XXII).
instrument.amendment_clause: Art. XXI: if a Power considers that its naval security requirements are materially affected by a change of circumstances, the Contracting Powers will at its request meet in conference "with a view to the reconsideration of the provisions of the Treaty and its amendment by mutual agreement". The United States, after consultation, is to arrange a conference of all Contracting Powers as soon as possible after eight years from entry into force to consider changes needed for technical and scientific developments. Art. XXII provides for a conference on the cessation of hostilities to consider modifications. The text sets no other amendment procedure.
instrument.entry_into_force_requirements: Ratification by all five Contracting Powers in accordance with their constitutional methods; the Treaty takes effect on the date of the deposit of all ratifications at Washington (Art. XXIV). The five instruments were deposited at the Department of State on 17 August 1923, recorded in a proces-verbal signed for the United States, the British Empire, France, Italy and Japan (UKTS 1924 No. 5, pp. 18-19). The United States Senate gave advice and consent on 29 March 1922 and the President ratified on 9 June 1923 (Bevans, vol. 2, p. 351).

I to XX), Chapter II (rules for execution, in four unnumbered Parts: Part 1 lists of retained capital ships, Part 2 scrapping rules, Part 3 replacement rules in Section I and replacement and scrapping tables in Section II, Part 4 definitions), Chapter III (Arts. XXI to XXIV). Word count: English text as printed in FRUS 1922, vol. I, pp. 247-266 (the United States text, Treaty Series No. 671), read from the Office of the Historian HTML, from "The United States of America, the British Empire" to the end of the dating formula ("Twenty-Two"), including the preamble, plenipotentiaries, headings, the notes printed below the tables and the note applicable to all the tables, and excluding the ten tables (the five Part 1 lists and the five Section II tables), the footnotes to those tables, signatures, editorial footnotes and the proces-verbal; whitespace tokens containing a letter or digit: 4,627. The UKTS print differs from the United States text in dating style (e.g. "the 12th November, 1921"; "Done at the City of Washington the 6th day of February, 1922"), changing the count by a few tokens.
instrument.weapons_systems_limited: Capital ships (defined for new construction as warships other than aircraft carriers over 10,000 tons standard displacement or with guns over 8 inches) and aircraft carriers, by named retained fleets, total replacement tonnage per Power, and per-ship displacement and gun calibre; all other warships by a per-ship ceiling of 10,000 tons and, for ships laid down after signature, an 8-inch gun limit. It also froze fortifications and naval bases of the United States, the British Empire and Japan in specified Pacific territories.
instrument.key_provisions: Each Power may retain the capital ships listed in Chapter II, Part 1; all other capital ships of the United States, the British Empire and Japan, built or building, are to be scrapped (Art. II). Capital ship building programmes are abandoned except for replacement under Chapter II, Part 3 (Art. III). Total capital ship replacement tonnage: United States and British Empire 525,000 tons each, Japan 315,000, France and Italy 175,000 each (Art. IV); no capital ship over 35,000 tons or with guns over 16 inches (Arts. V-VI). Aircraft carrier totals: 135,000 tons each for the United States and British Empire, 81,000 for Japan, 60,000 each for France and Italy (Art. VII); carriers limited to 27,000 tons, with two of up to 33,000 tons permitted, and to 8-inch guns (Arts. IX-X). No other warship over 10,000 tons, and no gun over 8 inches on non-capital ships laid down hereafter (Arts. XI-XII). Limits on reconversion, merchant ship preparation, construction for and transfer to other Powers (Arts. XIII-XVIII). Status quo on fortifications and naval bases in specified Pacific possessions of the United States, the British Empire and Japan (Art. XIX). Scrapping, replacement and notification rules and definitions (Chapter II). Conferences, wartime suspension, termination and ratification (Arts. XXI-XXIV).
instrument.behavior_change: The Treaty required existing forces to change: the United States, the British Empire and Japan were to scrap all capital ships, built or building, not on the retained lists (Art. II), within six months (disarming) and eighteen months (final scrapping) of entry into force (Ch. II, Part 2, para. IV(a)). It also closed future options for all five: building programmes were abandoned (Art. III), no capital ship tonnage other than specified replacements could be laid down until ten years from 12 November 1921 (Ch. II, Part 3, Section I(a)), and the three Pacific Powers gave up new fortifications and naval bases in listed possessions (Art. XIX). Hughes's proposal of 12 November 1921 counted 15 United States capital ships under construction among those to be scrapped (Senate Doc. 126, p. 47); in the Treaty's Japanese table, six capital ships of age zero and a projected programme of eight ships not laid down are listed for scrapping or abandonment (UKTS, p. 15). France and Italy kept their listed ships and scrapped only on replacement (Ch. II, Part 3, Section II).
instrument.historical_background: Secretary of State Charles Evans Hughes opened the Washington Conference on 12 November 1921 with a proposal to abandon capital ship building programmes, scrap built and building ships and fix capital ship strength on existing fleets in the ratio 5:5:3 for the United States, Britain and Japan (Senate Doc. 126, pp. 45-48). Japan's naval experts argued for 70 per cent; on 2 December Baron Kato linked acceptance of 60 per cent to a status quo on Pacific fortifications, and on 15 December the three Powers announced agreement on the 5:5:3 ratio and a fortifications status quo (FRUS 1922, vol. I, pp. 69-82, 127-129). France accepted the capital ship tonnage asked of it but refused corresponding reductions in light cruisers, torpedo boats and submarines (Briand to Hughes, 18 December 1921, FRUS 1922, vol. I, pp. 135-136). Hughes presented the Treaty to the fifth plenary session on 1 February 1922 and it was signed on 6 February 1922, the day the Conference closed (Senate Doc. 126, pp. 140-151, 231).

provisions.bound_parties_detail: Japan (one of three Powers bound by Art. XIX; France and Italy are not bound)
provisions.geographic_scope: The Kurile Islands, the Bonin Islands, Amami-Oshima, the Loochoo Islands, Formosa and the Pescadores, and any insular territories or possessions in the Pacific Ocean which Japan may hereafter acquire
provisions.exceptions: Repair and replacement of worn-out weapons and equipment customary in peacetime is permitted (Art. XIX, final sentence). The status quo is that at the time of signature (6 February 1922).
provisions.text_or_paraphrase: "The maintenance of the status quo under the foregoing provisions implies that no new fortifications or naval bases shall be established in the territories and possessions specified; that no measures shall be taken to increase the existing naval facilities for the repair and maintenance of naval forces, and that no increase shall be made in the coast defences of the territories and possessions above specified."

provisions.provision: Render ships due for scrapping incapable of warlike service within six months of entry into force
provisions.article: Ch. II, Part 2, paras. III and IV(a)
provisions.unit: months from entry into force (disarming of ships scrapped under Art. II, para. 1)
provisions.bound_parties_detail: The United States, the British Empire and Japan, whose surplus ships are scrapped under Art. II, para. 1
provisions.exceptions: Ships scrapped later on replacement must be disarmed within six months of the successor's completion, or, if the successor's completion is delayed, begun within four years of its keel-laying and finished within six months of beginning (para. IV(b)); carrier conversions under Art. IX are excepted (para. III(a)).
provisions.text_or_paraphrase: Para. III(b): a vessel is incapable of further warlike service when all guns and essential parts, fire-control tops and revolving parts of barbettes and turrets, hydraulic or electric mounting machinery, fire-control instruments and range-finders, ammunition, explosives and mines, torpedoes, warheads and tubes, wireless installations, the conning tower and all side armour (or all main propelling machinery), and all landing and flying-off platforms and aviation accessories have been removed and landed or destroyed. Para. IV(a): this work "shall be completed within six months from the coming into force of the present Treaty".

provisions.provision: Complete scrapping within eighteen months of entry into force
provisions.article: Ch. II, Part 2, paras. II and IV(a)
provisions.unit: months from entry into force (final scrapping of ships scrapped under Art. II, para. 1)
provisions.bound_parties_detail: The United States, the British Empire and Japan, whose surplus ships are scrapped under Art. II, para. 1
provisions.exceptions: Final scrapping is by permanent sinking, breaking up (removing or destroying all machinery, boilers, armour and plating) or conversion to target use; not more than one capital ship per Power may be kept as a target. France and Italy may each keep two ships otherwise scrapped in or after 1931 as training ships, after removing their conning-towers (para. II(d)). Ships replaced later are finally scrapped within eighteen months of the successor's completion or, if completion of the successor is delayed, within eighteen months from the date on which the work of rendering the old vessel incapable of further warlike service was commenced (para. IV(b)).
provisions.text_or_paraphrase: Para. IV(a): "the scrapping shall be finally effected within eighteen months from such coming into force."

provisions.provision: Replace capital ships and carriers only after twenty years of service
provisions.unit: years after completion before a capital ship or carrier may be replaced
provisions.bound_parties_detail: Every Contracting Power on identical terms
provisions.exceptions: Except as provided in Art. VIII (experimental carriers) and in the Section II tables; ships lost or accidentally destroyed may be replaced at once within the tonnage limits (Section I(c)). Within each year's quota a Power may vary the order of scrapping (note applicable to all the tables).
provisions.text_or_paraphrase: "Capital ships and aircraft carriers twenty years after the date of their completion may, except as otherwise provided in Article VIII and in the tables in Section II of this Part, be replaced by new construction, but within the limits prescribed in Article IV and Article VII."

provisions.provision: Lay replacement keels no earlier than seventeen years after completion of the ship replaced
provisions.unit: years after completion of the tonnage replaced before the replacement keel may be laid
provisions.bound_parties_detail: Every Contracting Power on identical terms
provisions.exceptions: Except as provided in Art. VIII and the Section II tables.
provisions.text_or_paraphrase: "The keels of such new construction may, except as otherwise provided in Article VIII and in the tables in Section II of this Part, be laid down not earlier than seventeen years from the date of completion of the tonnage to be replaced."

provisions.provision: Notify replacement construction of capital ships and aircraft carriers
provisions.bound_parties_detail: Every Contracting Power, to each of the other Contracting Powers
provisions.exceptions: None stated. No inspection or verification of the information is provided.
provisions.text_or_paraphrase: Each Power "shall communicate promptly to each of the other Contracting Powers": (1) the names of capital ships and carriers to be replaced; (2) the date of governmental authorisation of replacement tonnage; (3) the date of keel-laying; (4) the standard displacement and principal dimensions (waterline length, extreme beam, mean draft) of each new ship to be laid down; (5) the completion date, standard displacement and principal dimensions at completion.

provisions.provision: Reconstruction of retained capital ships and carriers limited to 3,000 tons of anti-air and anti-submarine protection
provisions.unit: tons added displacement per ship (3,048 metric tons)
provisions.bound_parties_detail: Every Contracting Power, with exceptions for France, Italy and the British Empire
provisions.exceptions: No alteration of side armour or of the calibre, number or general type of mounting of main armament, except that France and Italy may, within the bulge allowance, increase armour and raise the calibre of guns on existing capital ships up to 16 inches, and the British Empire may complete armour alterations already begun on the Renown.
provisions.text_or_paraphrase: "No retained capital ships or aircraft carriers shall be reconstructed except for the purpose of providing means of defence against air and submarine attack ... providing the increase of displacement thus effected does not exceed 3,000 tons (3,048 metric tons) displacement for each ship."

events.event: Hughes proposes a capital ship holiday, scrapping and the 5:5:3 ratio
events.actors: United States (Secretary of State Charles Evans Hughes); Conference on the Limitation of Armament
events.attribution: Address of the Secretary of State at the first plenary session, in Senate Doc. 126 (1922); text of the proposal in FRUS 1922, vol. I, doc. 34
events.description: Hughes proposed that all capital ship building programmes, actual or projected, be abandoned, that older ships be scrapped, that existing strength be the basis, and that capital ship tonnage measure naval strength, with a holiday of not less than ten years. The United States would scrap 15 capital ships under construction and 15 older battleships; Britain would stop four new Hoods and scrap older ships which, with some already scrapped, made 19; Japan would abandon ships not yet laid down and scrap 17 ships, leaving 500,650, 604,450 and 299,700 tons respectively. France's and Italy's allowances were reserved for later.
events.locator: Senate Doc. 126, pp. 45-48 (first plenary session, 12 November 1921)

events.event: Britain and Japan accept the American proposal in principle
events.actors: British Empire (Arthur James Balfour); Japan (Baron Tomosaburo Kato)
events.attribution: Speeches at the second plenary session, in Senate Doc. 126 (1922)
events.description: Balfour said the British Government thought "the proportion between the various countries is acceptable" and the limitation of amounts reasonable, while suggesting further limits on submarines. Kato said Japan, "Gladly accepting, therefore, the proposal in principle", was ready "to proceed with determination to a sweeping reduction in her naval armament", with modifications to be proposed on replacement tonnage.
events.locator: Senate Doc. 126, pp. 65-71 (second plenary session, 15 November 1921)

events.event: Japanese naval experts argue for a 70 per cent ratio
events.actors: Japan (naval experts under Vice Admiral Kato Kanji); United States naval experts
events.attribution: Memorandum by the Japanese naval experts and reply by the American naval experts, FRUS 1922, vol. I, docs. 43-44
events.description: The Japanese memorandum held that ships under construction were not existing strength and that on its calculations Japan had "about or over 70 per cent" of American strength; the American experts replied that the 15 United States ships under construction, averaging about 53 per cent complete, could not "be considered as non-existent".

events.event: Kato links acceptance of 60 per cent to a Pacific fortifications status quo
events.actors: Japan (Baron Kato); United States (Hughes); British Empire (Balfour)
events.attribution: British Empire Delegation record of a conversation at the Department of State, FRUS 1922, vol. I, doc. 46
events.description: Kato said it would help him accept the 60 per cent ratio if the United States agreed not to increase fortifications or naval bases at Guam, the Philippines and Hawaii, Japan in turn not fortifying Formosa, the Pescadores and Oshima. Hughes would consider a reciprocal status quo only as part of a general agreement and wished to exclude Hawaii as purely defensive.

events.event: United States, Britain and Japan announce agreement on the ratio and a fortifications status quo
events.actors: United States; British Empire; Japan
events.attribution: Statement issued to the press by the Conference, FRUS 1922, vol. I, doc. 57
events.description: The three Powers accepted the 5:5:3 ratio and a status quo on fortifications and naval bases in the Pacific, including Hong Kong, excluding Hawaii, Australia, New Zealand, the islands of Japan proper and the coasts of the United States and Canada. Japan would keep the Mutsu and scrap the Settsu; the United States would complete two ships and scrap the North Dakota and Delaware; Britain would build two new ships and scrap four; replacement maxima of 525,000, 525,000 and 315,000 tons and a 35,000-ton individual limit were set.

events.event: France accepts the capital ship allotment but not reductions in defensive ships
events.actors: France (Premier Aristide Briand); United States (Hughes)
events.attribution: Briand to Hughes, London, 18 December 1921 (translation), FRUS 1922, vol. I, doc. 62
events.description: Briand instructed the French delegates to accept the capital ship tonnage requested of them but wrote that for light cruisers, torpedo boats and submarines it would be impossible "to accept reductions corresponding to those which we accept for capital ships".

events.event: Hughes presents the naval treaty to the fifth plenary session
events.actors: Conference on the Limitation of Armament; United States (Hughes); France (Albert Sarraut)
events.attribution: Proceedings of the fifth plenary session, in Senate Doc. 126 (1922)
events.description: Hughes reported that agreement had been reached "which is embodied in a treaty now presented for your adoption" and summarised it, noting that the American proposals on auxiliary craft were not carried into it. Sarraut brought "the adhesion of the French Delegation". The printed proceedings consulted record the formal assent of the five delegations to the submarines and gases resolutions and treaty presented by Root; a separate vote on the naval treaty was not found in the scan.

events.event: Conference resolves that signatories are honour bound not to sell ships before ratification
events.actors: Signatory Powers of the naval treaty
events.attribution: Resolution adopted by the Conference on 4 February 1922, printed in Bevans, vol. 2
events.description: The resolution recorded that the Powers signatory of the Treaty of Naval Limitation "regard themselves in honor bound not to sell any ships between the present date and the ratification of the Treaty, when such a sale would be a breach of Article XVIII." Bevans gives it as effective between 4 February 1922 and 17 August 1923.

events.event: Treaty signed at the seventh plenary session
events.actors: United States, British Empire, France, Italy, Japan
events.attribution: Proceedings of the seventh plenary session, in Senate Doc. 126 (1922); dating formula of the Treaty
events.description: Hughes announced that the treaties approved by the Conference would be signed by the delegations in alphabetical order; the "Naval Treaty" was among the five treaties then signed by the respective delegations. The Treaty is dated "Done at the City of Washington the 6th day of February, 1922" and bears 20 signatures (Balfour signing twice), including those of the plenipotentiaries named for Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and India.
events.locator: Senate Doc. 126, p. 231; UKTS 1924 No. 5, p. 18

events.event: United States Senate gives advice and consent
events.actors: United States Senate
events.attribution: Bevans, vol. 2; FRUS 1922, vol. I, editorial note to doc. 77
events.description: Senate advice and consent to ratification. No reservation to this Treaty is noted in Bevans (the Four-Power Treaty carried one).

events.event: United States President ratifies
events.actors: United States (President Warren G. Harding)
events.attribution: Bevans, vol. 2; FRUS 1922, vol. I, editorial note to doc. 77
events.description: Ratification by the President of the United States. Ratification dates for the other four Powers were not found in the sources reviewed.

events.event: Ratifications deposited at Washington; Treaty enters into force
events.actors: United States (Charles Evans Hughes); British Empire (H. G. Chilton); France (Andre de Laboulaye); Italy (Augusto Rosso); Japan (M. Hanihara)
events.attribution: Proces-verbal of deposit of ratifications, printed in UKTS 1924 No. 5, Bevans and LNTS
events.description: At the Department of State at 12 o'clock, the representatives of the five Powers deposited the instruments of ratification, found to be in due form, with the United States Government. Under Art. XXIV the Treaty took effect on that date; Bevans records entry into force on 17 August 1923.
events.locator: UKTS 1924 No. 5, pp. 18-19; Bevans, vol. 2, pp. 351 and 371; LNTS vol. 25, pp. 226-227

events.event: France declares that the ratios do not reflect maritime interests and do not extend to other categories
events.actors: France
events.attribution: Declaration made at the deposit of ratifications, recorded in the proces-verbal
events.description: "The French Government considers and always has considered that the ratios of total tonnage in capital ships and aircraft carriers allowed to the several Contracting Powers do not represent the respective importance of the maritime interests of those Powers and cannot be extended to the categories of vessels other than those for which they were expressly stipulated." (Bevans translation; French original in UKTS.) France recalled the declaration on 2 January 1935.
events.locator: Bevans, vol. 2, p. 371; UKTS 1924 No. 5, p. 18

events.event: United States proclaims the Treaty
events.actors: United States (President)
events.attribution: Bevans, vol. 2
events.description: Proclamation by the President of the United States.

events.event: Treaty registered with the League of Nations
events.actors: British Empire (Foreign Office); League of Nations Secretariat
events.attribution: League of Nations Treaty Series, vol. 25
events.description: Registered as No. 609 on 16 April 1924; the official English and French texts were communicated by the British Foreign Office.

events.event: London Naval Treaty suspends capital ship replacement keel-laying for 1931-1936
events.actors: United States, France, United Kingdom (British Empire), Italy, Japan
events.attribution: Treaty for the Limitation and Reduction of Naval Armament (London Naval Treaty), Art. 1, printed in Bevans, vol. 2
events.description: The parties agreed "not to exercise their rights to lay down the keels of capital ship replacement tonnage during the years 1931-1936 inclusive as provided in Chapter II, Part 3" of the Washington Treaty, without prejudice to replacement of ships accidentally lost. The London Treaty is a separate instrument with its own record; Bevans gives its entry into force as 31 December 1930.

events.event: Japan gives notice of its intention to terminate the Treaty
events.actors: Japan (Ambassador Hirosi Saito); United States (Secretary of State Cordell Hull)
events.attribution: Memorandum by the Secretary of State of 29 December 1934 quoting Japanese Embassy note No. 250, FRUS 1934, vol. I, doc. 329; Bevans, vol. 2
events.description: Saito handed Hull a note giving notice under Art. XXIII of Japan's "intention to terminate the said Treaty, which will accordingly cease to be in force after the 31st December, 1936." Hull's memorandum describes the effect as that "Japan denounces the Washington Treaty". A note verbale stated Japan's policy of "discontinuance of the ratio system" and that it considered it "inadmissible to have the Treaty continue in force".
events.locator: FRUS 1934, vol. I, pp. 415-419; Bevans, vol. 2, p. 351, note 1

events.event: United States communicates the Japanese notice to the other Contracting Powers
events.actors: United States (Department of State); British Empire; France; Italy
events.attribution: Department circular of 29 December 1934 referred to in FRUS 1934, vol. I, docs. 331-333; Secretary of State press release, doc. 330
events.description: Hull replied orally that he would proceed under the Treaty to include Great Britain, France and Italy in the notice. His acknowledgment stated that, under Art. XXIII, he was transmitting a certified copy of the notification to the other Powers and informing them of the date of receipt. The text was delivered to the British Foreign Office on 31 December and communicated to the French Foreign Minister on 30 December. Hull's press statement said the Treaty's provisions "remain in force until the end of 1936".

events.event: France states its position on the Japanese notice
events.actors: France (Ambassador Andre de Laboulaye)
events.attribution: French Ambassador to the Secretary of State (translation), FRUS 1934, vol. I, doc. 332
events.description: France recalled its 1923 declaration, stated that the French Parliament had indicated that the Treaty "should come to an end on December 31, 1936", and said the French Government "would not have been able in any case to agree to its continuation". It considered that the Five Powers were obliged under Article 23 to meet in conference during 1935.

events.event: London Naval Conference opens
events.actors: United States, British Empire (United Kingdom), France, Italy, Japan
events.attribution: Chairman of the American Delegation (Norman Davis) to the Secretary of State, telegram No. 7, FRUS 1935, vol. I, doc. 151
events.description: "The London Naval Conference 1935 opened this morning at 10:30." France had described a conference in 1935 as an obligation under Art. XXIII; whether the Conference was formally convened under that article was not established in the sources reviewed.

events.event: Japanese delegation withdraws from the London Naval Conference
events.actors: Japan (Admiral Osami Nagano); Conference Chairman (Lord Monsell)
events.attribution: Nagano to Monsell, 15 January 1936, FRUS Japan 1931-1941, vol. I, doc. 213; press communique of the same day, doc. 212
events.description: After the First Committee found no support for Japan's proposal of a common upper limit, Nagano notified the Chairman that his delegation "can no longer usefully continue our participation in the deliberations of the present Conference" and could not subscribe to the plans of quantitative limitation of the other delegations.

events.event: Treaty terminates for all Contracting Powers
events.actors: United States, British Empire, France, Italy, Japan
events.attribution: Bevans, vol. 2; Japanese note of 29 December 1934 (FRUS 1934, vol. I)
events.description: Bevans records the Treaty as "Terminated December 31, 1936, in accordance with terms of article XXIII", following Japan's notice of 29 December 1934. Under Art. XXIII termination applies to all Contracting Powers.

participation.notes: Source label "the United States of America". Signed by Charles Evans Hughes, Henry Cabot Lodge, Oscar W. Underwood and Elihu Root. Date Signed 6 February 1922: the seventh plenary session record states that the delegations signed the Naval Treaty in alphabetical order that day (Senate Doc. 126, p. 231), and the Treaty is dated 6 February 1922 (UKTS 1924 No. 5, p. 18). Senate advice and consent 29 March 1922; ratified by the President 9 June 1923; proclaimed 21 August 1923 (Bevans, vol. 2, p. 351). Entry into Force 17 August 1923, the date of the deposit of all ratifications at Washington (Art. XXIV; proces-verbal, UKTS 1924 No. 5, pp. 18-19; Bevans, vol. 2, p. 351). Depositary of the Treaty (Art. XXIV) and recipient of Japan's notice of termination (FRUS 1934, vol. I, pp. 415-416). The Treaty terminated for all Contracting Powers on 31 December 1936 under Art. XXIII after Japan's notice of 29 December 1934 (Bevans, vol. 2, p. 351); no current status is coded.

Source label "the British Empire", kept as the depositary record and the Treaty give it; not linked to the United Kingdom and no continuity is coded. The High Contracting Party is His Majesty the King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and of the British Dominions beyond the Seas, Emperor of India, whose plenipotentiaries were Balfour, Lee of Fareham and Geddes "and for the Dominion of Canada" Borden, for Australia Pearce, for New Zealand Salmond, for South Africa Balfour and for India Srinivasa Sastri (preamble and signatures, UKTS 1924 No. 5, pp. 2-3, 18). One row is coded because the Treaty names the British Empire as a single Contracting Power (preamble; Arts. II, IV, VII, XIX) and the proces-verbal records one ratification deposited "For the British Empire" by H. G. Chilton (UKTS, p. 19; Bevans, vol. 2, p. 371); no separate Dominion or Indian ratifications appear in the sources reviewed. Bevans adds editorial labels such as "[For the Dominion of Canada:]" to the signature blocks. The British Foreign Office communicated the texts for League registration (LNTS vol. 25, p. 202). Date Signed 6 February 1922: the seventh plenary session record states that the delegations signed the Naval Treaty in alphabetical order that day (Senate Doc. 126, p. 231), and the Treaty is dated 6 February 1922 (UKTS 1924 No. 5, p. 18). The date of the British instrument of ratification was not found. Entry into Force 17 August 1923, the date of the deposit of all ratifications at Washington (Art. XXIV; proces-verbal, UKTS 1924 No. 5, pp. 18-19; Bevans, vol. 2, p. 351). The Treaty terminated for all Contracting Powers on 31 December 1936 under Art. XXIII after Japan's notice of 29 December 1934 (Bevans, vol. 2, p. 351); no current status is coded.

Source label "France" (the President of the French Republic). Signed by Albert Sarraut and Jules J. Jusserand. Date Signed 6 February 1922: the seventh plenary session record states that the delegations signed the Naval Treaty in alphabetical order that day (Senate Doc. 126, p. 231), and the Treaty is dated 6 February 1922 (UKTS 1924 No. 5, p. 18). The date of the French instrument of ratification was not found; a French note of 2 January 1935 says Parliament, in considering ratification, intended the Treaty to end on 31 December 1936, citing Chamber of Deputies debates of 7 July 1923 (FRUS 1934, vol. I, p. 422 and note 75). At the deposit France declared that the capital ship and carrier ratios did not represent the Powers' maritime interests and could not be extended to other categories of vessels (proces-verbal, Bevans, vol. 2, p. 371). Entry into Force 17 August 1923, the date of the deposit of all ratifications at Washington (Art. XXIV; proces-verbal, UKTS 1924 No. 5, pp. 18-19; Bevans, vol. 2, p. 351). The Treaty terminated for all Contracting Powers on 31 December 1936 under Art. XXIII after Japan's notice of 29 December 1934 (Bevans, vol. 2, p. 351); no current status is coded.

Source label "Italy" (His Majesty the King of Italy). Signed by Carlo Schanzer, Vittorio Rolandi Ricci and Luigi Albertini. Date Signed 6 February 1922: the seventh plenary session record states that the delegations signed the Naval Treaty in alphabetical order that day (Senate Doc. 126, p. 231), and the Treaty is dated 6 February 1922 (UKTS 1924 No. 5, p. 18). The date of the Italian instrument of ratification was not found; Augusto Rosso signed the proces-verbal of deposit. Entry into Force 17 August 1923, the date of the deposit of all ratifications at Washington (Art. XXIV; proces-verbal, UKTS 1924 No. 5, pp. 18-19; Bevans, vol. 2, p. 351). The Treaty terminated for all Contracting Powers on 31 December 1936 under Art. XXIII after Japan's notice of 29 December 1934 (Bevans, vol. 2, p. 351); no current status is coded.

Source label "Japan" (His Majesty the Emperor of Japan). Signed by Baron Tomosaburo Kato, Baron Kijuro Shidehara and Masanao Hanihara. Date Signed 6 February 1922: the seventh plenary session record states that the delegations signed the Naval Treaty in alphabetical order that day (Senate Doc. 126, p. 231), and the Treaty is dated 6 February 1922 (UKTS 1924 No. 5, p. 18). The date of the Japanese instrument of ratification was not found; M. Hanihara signed the proces-verbal of deposit. Entry into Force 17 August 1923, the date of the deposit of all ratifications at Washington (Art. XXIV; proces-verbal, UKTS 1924 No. 5, pp. 18-19; Bevans, vol. 2, p. 351). overview_md: The Washington Naval Treaty of 6 February 1922 limited the capital ships and aircraft carriers of the United States, the British Empire, France, Italy and Japan. It fixed the capital ships each Power could keep, required the United States, the British Empire and Japan to scrap the rest, built or building, set total replacement tonnage of 525,000 tons each for the United States and the British Empire, 315,000 for Japan and 175,000 each for France and Italy, capped new capital ships at 35,000 tons and 16-inch guns, and limited the acquisition and construction of other warships to 10,000 tons, excluding aircraft carriers and the auxiliary vessels specified in Article XI ([UKTS 1924 No. 5](https://treaties.fcdo.gov.uk/data/Library2/pdf/1924-TS0005.pdf)). Article XIX froze fortifications and naval bases of the United States, the British Empire and Japan in specified Pacific territories. The only information obligations are notifications of replacement construction and of warships built for other Powers; the text creates no inspection. The Treaty entered into force on 17 August 1923 and terminated for all parties on 31 December 1936 after Japan gave notice on 29 December 1934 ([Bevans, vol. 2, p. 351](https://tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/ll/lltreaties/lltreaties-ustbv002/lltreaties-ustbv002.pdf); [FRUS 1934, vol. I](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1934v01/d329)).
provisions_md:
Citations are to [UK Treaty Series 1924 No. 5](https://treaties.fcdo.gov.uk/data/Library2/pdf/1924-TS0005.pdf), checked against the United States text in [FRUS 1922, vol. I](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1922v01/d77) and [Bevans, vol. 2](https://tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/ll/lltreaties/lltreaties-ustbv002/lltreaties-ustbv002.pdf); French and English texts are equally authentic (Art. XXIV).

### Capital ships
- Each Power may retain the capital ships listed in Chapter II, Part 1. All other capital ships of the United States, the British Empire and Japan, built or building, are to be scrapped (Art. II). The United States may complete two West Virginia class ships and then scraps the North Dakota and Delaware; the British Empire may build two ships of up to 35,000 tons and then scraps four older ships.
- Building programmes are abandoned; new capital ships may be built or acquired only as replacement tonnage (Art. III). No capital ship keel may be laid until ten years from 12 November 1921, except the two British ships and the tonnage listed in the replacement tables, which let France and Italy lay down ships in 1927, 1929 and 1931 (Ch. II, Part 3, Section I(a)).
- Total replacement tonnage: United States 525,000 tons; British Empire 525,000; Japan 315,000; France 175,000; Italy 175,000 (Art. IV). No capital ship over 35,000 tons or with a gun over 16 inches (Arts. V-VI).
- Replacement is allowed 20 years after completion, with keels laid no earlier than 17 years after completion (Section I(a)). Reconstruction is limited to 3,000 tons of anti-air and anti-submarine protection, with exceptions for France, Italy and the Renown (Section I(d)).

### Aircraft carriers
- Total carrier tonnage: 135,000 tons each for the United States and the British Empire, 81,000 for Japan, 60,000 each for France and Italy (Art. VII). Existing carriers are experimental and replaceable regardless of age (Art. VIII).
- No carrier over 27,000 tons, but each Power may build two of up to 33,000 tons, including from two hulls otherwise due for scrapping (Art. IX). No carrier gun over 8 inches, with limits on the number of guns over 6 inches (Arts. IX-X).

### Other warships, merchant ships and transfers
- No other vessel of war over 10,000 tons, and no gun over 8 inches on non-capital ships laid down after signature (Arts. XI-XII). The number and total tonnage of cruisers, destroyers and submarines are not limited.
- No reconversion of ships designated for scrapping; no peacetime preparation of merchant ships for armament beyond deck stiffening for guns up to 6 inches (Arts. XIII-XIV).
- Warships built for non-Contracting Powers must respect the Treaty limits and their construction must be notified; a Power at war may not use ships built for others; no Power may transfer a warship so that it may join a foreign navy (Arts. XV-XVIII).

### Pacific fortifications and bases (Art. XIX)
- Binds only the United States, the British Empire and Japan, each keeping the status quo of 6 February 1922 in listed areas: United States Pacific islands other than those near its coasts, Alaska and the Panama Canal Zone (the Aleutians are covered) and Hawaii; Hong Kong and British Pacific islands east of 110 degrees east other than those near Canada, Australia and its territories, and New Zealand; and the Kuriles, Bonins, Amami-Oshima, Loochoo Islands, Formosa, the Pescadores and future Japanese Pacific acquisitions. No new fortifications or naval bases and no increase in repair facilities or coast defences; customary repair of worn-out equipment is allowed.

### Scrapping
- Ships scrapped on entry into force are disarmed within six months and finally scrapped within 18 months, by sinking, breaking up or conversion to a target (one per Power); France and Italy may keep two training ships (Ch. II, Part 2).

### Information and verification
- Each Power must promptly communicate to the others the ships to be replaced, the dates of authorisation, keel-laying and completion, and the displacement and principal dimensions of new ships (Section I(b)), and must notify construction for non-Contracting Powers (Art. XVI). The text creates no inspection, verification body or enforcement procedure.

### Conferences and suspension
- Conferences on request after a material change of circumstances, and on technical developments after eight years (Art. XXI); wartime suspension after notice, except Arts. XIII and XVII (Art. XXII).
participation_md:
- **Parties.** Closed to the five signatory Powers; there is no accession clause. The British Empire is one Contracting Power; plenipotentiaries for Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and India signed for it, and one British ratification was deposited ([UKTS 1924 No. 5](https://treaties.fcdo.gov.uk/data/Library2/pdf/1924-TS0005.pdf), pp. 2-3, 18-19).
- **Signature.** Signed at Washington by all five delegations at the seventh plenary session of the Conference on 6 February 1922 ([Senate Doc. 126](https://archive.org/details/conferenceonlim00hardgoog), p. 231).
- **Ratification and entry into force.** Ratification by all five in accordance with their constitutional methods; the Treaty took effect on the deposit of all ratifications at Washington (Art. XXIV), on 17 August 1923. France made a declaration on the ratios at the deposit. The United States Senate consented on 29 March 1922 and the President ratified on 9 June 1923 ([Bevans, vol. 2](https://tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/ll/lltreaties/lltreaties-ustbv002/lltreaties-ustbv002.pdf), pp. 351, 371). Registered with the League of Nations as No. 609 on 16 April 1924 ([LNTS vol. 25](https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/LON/Volume%2025/v25.pdf)).
- **Duration and termination.** In force until 31 December 1936, continuing afterwards until two years after any Power's notice of termination, which ends the Treaty for all (Art. XXIII). Japan's notice of 29 December 1934 ended it on 31 December 1936 ([FRUS 1934, vol. I](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1934v01/d329); Bevans, p. 351).
- **Suspension.** A Power at war affecting its naval defence may suspend its obligations, other than Arts. XIII and XVII, after notice (Art. XXII). No invocation was identified in the sources reviewed.
- **Amendment and review.** Conferences on request and amendment by mutual agreement; a conference on technical developments after eight years; a conference after hostilities; and a conference of all Powers within one year of a termination notice taking effect (Arts. XXI-XXIII).
- **Depositary.** The Government of the United States.
history_md:
### Negotiation
Hughes opened the Washington Conference on 12 November 1921 by proposing that capital ship programmes be abandoned, built and building ships scrapped, and capital ship strength fixed on existing fleets for the United States, Britain and Japan ([Senate Doc. 126](https://archive.org/details/conferenceonlim00hardgoog), pp. 45-48). Balfour and Baron Kato accepted the proposal in principle on 15 November (pp. 65-71). Japan's naval experts argued that ships under construction were not existing strength and that Japan was entitled to about 70 per cent ([FRUS 1922, vol. I, doc. 43](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1922v01/d43)). On 2 December Kato said a status quo on Pacific fortifications would help him accept 60 per cent ([doc. 46](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1922v01/d46)), and on 15 December the three Powers announced the 5:5:3 ratio, the fortifications status quo and the exchange that let Japan keep the Mutsu ([doc. 57](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1922v01/d57)). Premier Briand accepted the capital ship tonnage asked of France but refused corresponding reductions in light cruisers, torpedo boats and submarines ([Briand to Hughes, doc. 62](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1922v01/d62)); Andrade attributes the absence of auxiliary limits mainly to French opposition ([Andrade 1969](https://www.jstor.org/stable/24440557), pp. 358-359). Hughes presented the Treaty on 1 February 1922, and it was signed on 6 February (Senate Doc. 126, pp. 140-151, 231).

### Ratification and implementation
Ratifications were deposited on 17 August 1923, with a French declaration that the ratios did not reflect maritime interests and could not extend to other categories ([Bevans, vol. 2](https://tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/ll/lltreaties/lltreaties-ustbv002/lltreaties-ustbv002.pdf), p. 371). Andrade reports that the United States converted the battle cruisers Lexington and Saratoga, and Japan the Kaga and Akagi, into carriers under Art. IX (p. 358). By the London Naval Treaty of 1930 the five Powers agreed not to lay down capital ship replacement tonnage in 1931-1936 (Bevans, vol. 2, p. 1057).

### Termination
On 29 December 1934 Ambassador Saito handed Secretary Hull Japan's notice under Art. XXIII; Hull recorded that Japan "denounces the Washington Treaty", and a Japanese note verbale cited the "discontinuance of the ratio system" ([FRUS 1934, vol. I, doc. 329](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1934v01/d329)). The United States informed the other Powers, and France replied that it could not have agreed to the Treaty's continuation ([doc. 332](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1934v01/d332)). The London Naval Conference opened on 9 December 1935 ([FRUS 1935, vol. I, doc. 151](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1935v01/d151)); the Japanese delegation withdrew on 15 January 1936 ([FRUS Japan 1931-1941, vol. I, doc. 213](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1931-41v01/d213)). The Treaty terminated on 31 December 1936 (Bevans, p. 351). Asada links Japan's course to naval opposition to the 60 per cent ratio ([Asada 1993](https://www.jstor.org/stable/44637473), pp. 82, 94).

### Compliance
No formal allegation of violation by a Contracting Power, and no finding, was identified in the sources reviewed. Claims of displacement overruns found in unofficial secondary material were not verified and are not recorded.

coding_notes.note: Treaty/Convention: the parties call it a treaty, it is subject to ratification (Art. XXIV) and it is published in the United States Treaty Series (No. 671), the UK Treaty Series (1924 No. 5) and the League of Nations Treaty Series (vol. 25, No. 609).
Legally binding, from the text (ratification and deposit, Art. XXIV; termination only on notice, Art. XXIII) and its registration and publication in official treaty series.

6 February 1922, the date the Treaty bears ("Done at the City of Washington the 6th day of February, 1922") and the day it was signed at the seventh plenary session (Senate Doc. 126, p. 231). Hughes presented it to the fifth plenary session on 1 February 1922; a formal adoption vote on the naval treaty was not found in the proceedings consulted, so that date is recorded as an event, not as adoption.

Coded 6 February 1922 because the proceedings record that all five delegations signed that day (Senate Doc. 126, p. 231). The Treaty was not opened for later signature; no Opening for signature event is recorded, so the key facts show this date as the signature date.

17 August 1923: Art. XXIV makes the Treaty take effect on the deposit of all ratifications; the proces-verbal of deposit is dated 17 August 1923 (UKTS 1924 No. 5, p. 19; LNTS vol. 25, p. 227) and Bevans records entry into force on that date (vol. 2, p. 351). The UKTS cover calls this an exchange of ratifications; the proces-verbal itself records a deposit with the United States Government.

31 December 1936, as recorded by Bevans ("Terminated December 31, 1936, in accordance with terms of article XXIII", vol. 2, p. 351) and as stated in Japan's notice ("cease to be in force after the 31st December, 1936", FRUS 1934, vol. I, p. 416). Hull's memorandum of the same day speaks of termination "on January 1st, 1937"; the last day in force and the first day after are the same end point. The date was taken from these sources, not computed.
Terminated, following Bevans ("Terminated ... in accordance with terms of article XXIII").

Denunciation: the Treaty ended because Japan gave notice of termination under Art. XXIII (FRUS 1934, vol. I, pp. 415-416); Secretary Hull recorded that "Japan denounces the Washington Treaty", and the French note of 2 January 1935 also speaks of denunciation. Under Art. XXIII the notice took effect on the date it was received, 29 December 1934, and the Treaty terminated for all Powers on 31 December 1936. Denunciation is kept because the end depended on a party's notice, which ended the Treaty for all parties rather than withdrawing one Power.
Plurilateral (closed): the five Powers are named in the preamble and the text has no accession or adhesion clause.
Left empty (worldwide): the ship limits apply wherever the Powers' navies are. Art. XIX applies only in specified Pacific territories; its areas are recorded in the provision rows.
Sea for the ship limits and merchant ship rules; Land for the Art. XIX freeze on fortifications, naval bases, repair facilities and coast defences in island territories.
Naval forces (capital ships, carriers, all vessels of war); Fortifications & bases (Art. XIX). Aircraft carriers are naval forces; the Treaty does not limit aircraft.

Arms limitation & disarmament (ceilings, scrapping); Arms trade & transfer control (Arts. XV-XVIII on construction for and transfer to other Powers). Art. XIX freezes existing installations and requires no removal, so it is not coded as a demilitarized zone.

Notifications, from the text only: Ch. II, Part 3, Section I(b) requires each Power to communicate promptly to the others the names of ships to be replaced, dates of authorisation, keel-laying and completion, and the standard displacement and principal dimensions of each new ship; Art. XVI requires notice of construction for non-Contracting Powers. These are event-driven communications, not periodic reports or a baseline declaration. Vaynman's dataset codes this treaty (code 1922.3, "Washington Conference on the Limitation of Armament") as information level low, type "reporting"; that is context only and did not drive this code.
None: the text creates no inspection, observation or verification body.
None specified: the text does not mention national means or any other means of monitoring.
Yes under the codebook definition (parties must submit data to another party): Ch. II, Part 3, Section I(b) and Art. XVI. Coded from the instrument's own text.
Not specified in text: no consequence for non-compliance is provided. Art. XXII suspension is tied to a party's engagement in war, not to another party's breach. Coded from the instrument's own text.
Not specified in text: Art. XXI conferences concern changed circumstances and technical developments, not disputes over interpretation or application. Coded from the instrument's own text.
Not specified in text. Coded from the instrument's own text.
Not specified in text. Coded from the instrument's own text.

Not specified in text: Arts. XV-XVIII restrict what Contracting Powers may build for or transfer to non-Contracting Powers but assign no function to any non-party; the United States Government acts as depositary as a party. Coded from the instrument's own text.

Consultative meetings: Art. XXI provides for conferences at a Power's request and a conference on technical developments; Art. XXII for consultation among the remaining Powers when one suspends in war and for a conference after hostilities; Art. XXIII for a conference within one year of a termination notice taking effect. There is no standing body.
Depositary only: the United States Government receives ratifications and termination notices and transmits copies (Arts. XXIII-XXIV).

Not Specified: the text does not address reservations. France's declaration at the deposit concerns the meaning and extension of the ratios and is recorded as an event; the proces-verbal does not call it a reservation, and Bevans notes no United States reservation to this Treaty.

Fixed term (renewable): the Treaty runs to 31 December 1936 and, absent notice two years before, continues automatically until two years after any notice (Art. XXIII). Duration (years) is left blank because the term is fixed by a date, not a number of years.

Notice, with 24 months: a notice of termination by any Power ends the Treaty for all, two years after the notice or on 31 December 1936 for a notice given at least two years before (Art. XXIII). There is no separate withdrawal of one Power. Art. XXII wartime suspension is described in the withdrawal clause.
Unanimity, read from Art. XXI: amendment is "by mutual agreement" of the Contracting Powers in conference; the text uses neither word "unanimity" nor "consensus".

Ad hoc / on request: Art. XXI provides conferences at a Power's request and a single conference on technical developments after eight years from entry into force; it sets no periodic cycle, so Review Interval is blank.

Left blank. No source reviewed establishes that the Art. XXI eight-year conference was convened as such. The 1927 Geneva conference and the 1930 London conference were separate negotiations, and the 1935-1936 London conference followed Japan's termination notice, which France linked to Art. XXIII; none is counted as a review conference here.

Left blank: the Treaty terminated on 31 December 1936 and has no current parties. Historical count: 5 Contracting Powers, all of which signed on 6 February 1922 and ratified, deposited 17 August 1923 (list checked 12 October 2026).
5 Contracting Powers. The British Empire is counted once although plenipotentiaries for Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and India also signed (20 signatures in all).
Official text: UK Treaty Series 1924 No. 5 (the local PDF is byte-identical to the FCDO file), checked against LNTS vol. 25 and the United States text in FRUS 1922, vol. I and Bevans, vol. 2.

Produced by the Washington Conference (AC-2); negotiated alongside the Submarines and Noxious Gases Treaty (AC-68), the Four-Power Treaty and the Nine-Power Treaty (no rows; listed as missing). The London Naval Treaties of 1930 and 1936 are later instruments and carry their own relations.

unverified.reason: Dates of the British, French, Italian and Japanese instruments of ratification were not found; only the common deposit date (17 August 1923) and the United States dates are documented.
The proceedings scan does not show a separate vote approving the naval treaty at the fifth plenary session; adoption is coded at signature.
No source reviewed shows the Art. XXI eight-year technical conference being convened as such, or the 1935-1936 London conference being formally convened under Art. XXIII.

Claims on the old page (from Wikipedia) that France and Italy violated displacement or tonnage limits, that Britain objected, and that the United States counted 3,000 tons of reconstruction allowance for Lexington and Saratoga were not verified in official or scholarly sources opened and are not recorded.
The Kaga, Akagi, Lexington and Saratoga conversions are reported from Andrade (1969) only; no primary source was opened.
Participation of the five Powers in the 1935-1936 conference is inferred from FRUS document titles; the opening telegram does not list delegations. The 25 March 1936 London Treaty was not opened.
